sustainable-innovation/00-concept-sustai.t: Concept of Sustainable Innovation (Circular, Frugal, Social)

q.q: Which statement fits Schumpeter’s distinction?
options: Innovation is the realization of a new resource
Invention is the integration of a resource in a product offered to the market
Invention is the realization of a new resource; innovation is its integration in an offer to the market
q.explain: Slide 7.

q.q: According to Kim & Mauborgne, radical innovations represent 14% of innovations and generate:
q.explain: Disproportionate impact of radical innovation.

q.q: In the A.D. Little matrix, a function extension (e.g. remote control for TV) is:
q.explain: Function extension is shown as incremental; market extension is radical.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the three criteria for frugal innovation (Weyrauch & Herstatt)?
q.explain: Sustainable and scalable are possible additional characteristics, not defining ones.

q.q: Why are cheap tablets in developed markets NOT frugal innovations?
options: They meet only criterion 1; they keep similar functions and their performance is not optimised
q.explain: They are simply cost innovations.

q.q: The MittiCool is judged frugal because:
options: It meets all 3 criteria (≈60% cheaper, core cooling function, adapted performance)
It is sold in large numbers
q.explain: Article Fig. 4.

q.q: Which are the Ellen MacArthur Foundation’s circular economy principles?
options: Preserve natural capital, optimize resource use, eliminate negative externalities
q.explain: Slide 31 / Suchek et al.

q.q: According to the Quebec Declaration, the main pitfalls to implementing innovation are rarely:
q.explain: They are usually organizational, social or cultural.

q.q: Which dynamic of social innovation involves involving future users in design?
q.explain: Citizen dimension.

q.q: Why does Suchek et al. insist on radical rather than incremental eco-innovation?
options: Incremental innovation may be susceptible to rebound effects
q.explain: Conclusion section.

sociology-social-transformations-managem.t: AI vs Human Judgment & Introduction to Sociology

q.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Phronēsis: practical wisdom AI cannot supply
q.explain: Technē is the “how” that AI scales; phronēsis is practical wisdom.

q.q: According to Simon (as used in the course), what can a machine NOT tell you?
options: Whether the objective you gave it is the right one
q.explain: The machine optimizes the objective it is given.

q.q: What does the Zillow Offers case illustrate?
q.explain: The algorithm hit its target (predicted price) almost perfectly; the target was wrong as the market turned.

q.q: In the Air Canada case, the tribunal held that:
options: The company owns whatever its systems tell customers
q.explain: Responsibility stays human.

q.q: For Arendt, thinking differs from cognition because it is:
options: The inner dialogue where we judge meaning and right from wrong
q.explain: Machines do cognition (problem-solving).

q.q: Which concept comes from Durkheim?
q.explain: Iron cage = Weber; habitus = Bourdieu; zone of uncertainty = Crozier & Friedberg.

q.q: Holism is the heir of:
q.explain: Holism ← realism; methodological individualism ← nominalism.

q.q: A sales force paid only on volume floods customers with products they return. Which reading and author fit best?
q.explain: No structure forced it: individual rational choices produced an unwanted collective result.

q.q: “Gut feel” in hiring being habitus recognizing its own kind illustrates:
q.explain: Habitus is the managerial hook given for Bourdieu.

q.q: What is the “diagnostic habit” proposed at the end?
options: Ask the problem twice, with the holist and the individualist grid
q.explain: The richest analysis lives in the tension between the grids.

q.q: According to the course, what makes an innovation sustainable?
options: Consistency between value proposition, value chain and business model and the sustainability objective
A strong marketing campaign about its green features
q.explain: Key message of session 2: a better product alone is not enough.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the 5 steps of design thinking shown in the course?
q.explain: Steps: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.

q.q: In Orangebox case B (Cors), durability and recyclability were achieved by moulding a nylon seat over a steel frame, but manual disassembly was sacrificed. Which dilemma type is this in the case table?
q.explain: Table 8 classes case B as hierarchies: durability and recyclability work in tandem yet preclude intact part disassembly.

q.q: Case C: the chair designed as the ‘most environmental chair’ via C2C had higher LCA impact than cases A and D. This is a:
q.explain: LCA results and C2C guidance appear contradictory.

q.q: Baldassarre et al. found that in 115 design thinking articles, the share dealing with environmental impact was about:
q.explain: 8 articles of 115 (7%); economic 90%, social 40%.

q.q: In responsible design thinking, ‘inclusive co-creating’ corresponds to which responsible innovation dimension and outcome?
q.explain: Development phase: co-creating ↔ inclusion ↔ coalitions of organisations.

q.q: Why does the Accor example say DT is hard in many organisations?
options: It is incompatible with the top-down managerial culture that often prevails
q.explain: DT relies on trust and recognising teams’ competence.

q.q: According to Prendeville et al., what do the authors say the business model does for ecodesign?
q.explain: Case C: the chair was high-impact in a direct-sales model where life cycles are not managed.

consumer-behavior-customer-experience-ma.t: From Understanding Consumers to Designing Experiences

q.q: Which decision type skips the search and evaluation stages?
q.explain: Habitual: “I just do what I usually do”; the decision has been made by past behaviour.

q.q: A heavy smoker knows smoking causes cancer but keeps smoking, then downplays the risk. This is:
q.explain: Festinger (1957): out-of-sync A, B and C create tension we resolve by adjusting one.

q.q: Involvement shapes mainly:
options: Information search, perceived differences among alternatives, deliberation time and price sensitivity
q.explain: It acts on search and evaluation.

q.q: According to McCracken (1986), meaning moves:
q.explain: Culture to brand (advertising, design), then brand to consumer (use, wear, talk).

q.q: “Am I buying less, better, and with less impact?” is the question of:
q.explain: Responsible consumption is the narrower, environment-focused concept.

q.q: For Holbrook & Corfman (1985), an experience results from:
q.explain: Hence it is singular and the consumer is its true producer.

q.q: Which is NOT a feature of extraordinary experiences?
q.explain: Intensity, engagement, temporality (Scott, Cayla & Cova, 2017).

q.q: Descending the Grand Canyon (active participation and immersion) is, for Pine & Gilmore:
q.explain: Esthetic = merely viewing from the rim.

q.q: Lemon & Verhoef’s touchpoints include customer reviews and word of mouth. They are:
q.explain: Brand-owned: ads, website, app; partner-owned: co-marketing, delivery; customer-owned: their own choices, habits.

q.q: Which statement matches the course AI policy?
options: AI is allowed in the final exam
AI is permitted for the group project only, if transparent; not for in-class case studies or the exam
AI is allowed for case studies but not the project
q.explain: Any AI use must be acknowledged and logged; the fieldwork must be your own.

corporate-financial-decisions/01-time-va.t: Time Value of Money, Loans & Amortization

q.q: €100 invested for 3 years at 10% with COMPOUND interest gives:
q.explain: 100 × 1.10³ = 133.10. €130 would be simple interest (€10 per year).

q.q: What is the present value of €100 received in 2 years at 10%?
q.explain: 100 / 1.10² = 82.64 (90.90 is for one year only).

q.q: According to the Fisher effect, a lender wants a 4% real return and expects 6% inflation. The nominal rate is about:
q.explain: Nominal = real + expected inflation = 4% + 6%.

q.q: Which statement about APR and EAR is correct?
options: EAR is the rate used to derive the monthly rate
The APR is the rate you really pay each year
The EAR is bigger than the APR when there is compounding within the year
q.explain: The APR is used to derive the periodic rate; the EAR is the rate actually paid per year, which is bigger because of compounding.

q.q: A credit card charges 0.05% per day. The APR is:
q.explain: APR = periodic rate × 365 = 18.25%. (20.02% would be the EAR.)

q.q: Loan of €10,000, 5 years, APR 5%, monthly payments. Which inputs for the payment function?
q.explain: Periodic rate = APR/12 and n = years × 12.

q.q: In an amortization schedule with a constant payment, over time:
q.explain: Interest = beginning balance × rate, and the balance falls, so principal = payment − interest rises.

q.q: In the loan contract of the course, “8 342,64 euros” is:
q.explain: 36 × 231.74 = 8,342.64 is the total to repay.

q.q: In anthropology, a myth is:
options: A foundational narrative giving origin, identity and direction
q.explain: Its truth is meaning-bearing, not factual.

q.q: Which function is NOT one of the four functions of rites in the course?
q.explain: Integration, cohesion, legitimacy, safe transition.

q.q: The three phases of a rite of passage (van Gennep) are:
q.explain: Liminality is the in-between threshold.

q.q: Mauss’s triple obligation of the gift is:
q.explain: The gift is a total social fact that weaves the social bond.

q.q: A company officially values “speak up”, but a manager who challenged the CEO is quietly removed. In Bourdieu’s terms the manager’s challenge is closest to:
q.explain: Heterodoxy = challenge and dissent. (The slide asks the question without giving an official answer; this follows Bourdieu’s definitions.)

q.q: Which is Schein’s deepest, invisible level?
q.explain: The iceberg: real culture lives below the waterline.

q.q: Warning on micro-rites: if you “delete meetings”…
options: People recreate the rite elsewhere; replace the function, not just the form
q.explain: Goffman’s micro-rites quietly sustain cohesion.

q.q: What does the Danone case illustrate?
options: Doctrine is power and is contested (stakeholder purpose vs shareholder value)
q.explain: Loi PACTE 2019; Faber ousted in 2021.

q.q: Durkheim’s collective effervescence is best illustrated in the course by:
q.explain: Engineered Durkheimian energy that recharges belonging.

q.q: Girard’s pattern is:
q.explain: The expulsion of the victim restores unity; founding myths often conceal it.

q.q: Project A: WACC 10%, CFs −100, 10, 60, 80. The NPV is about:
q.explain: 10/1.1 + 60/1.21 + 80/1.331 − 100 = 118.78 − 100 ≈ 18.78 (the course shows 18.79 with rounded PVs). Positive → accept.

q.q: A project has an IRR of 9.49% and a required return of 7%. Decision?
options: Reject: IRR is above the hurdle rate
q.explain: Accept when IRR > discount rate; NPV is then positive at 7%.

q.q: Why does the course recommend the NPV rule over the IRR rule?
options: IRR ignores the time value of money
IRR may have several algebraic solutions
IRR is harder to compute in Excel
NPV always gives a higher value
q.explain: Solving for IRR may lead to several possible solutions.

q.q: Limited budget of $300,000: A (200k, PI 2.15), B (125k, 2.13), C (175k, 2.11), D (150k, 2.08). The best selection is:
q.explain: WAPI(BC)=2.12 > WAPI(BD)=1.93 > WAPI(A)=1.43. (A and D would cost 350k.)

q.q: Payback for CFs −100, 70, 50, 20:
q.explain: After year 1 cumulative = −30; year 2 CF = 50 → 1 + 30/50 = 1.6.

q.q: Which is a weakness of the (simple) payback?
options: It ignores the time value of money
q.explain: Payback ignores TVM and CFs after the payback period.

q.q: In Excel, the correct NPV with CF0 in B2 and CF1…CFn in B3:B12 is:
q.explain: NPV discounts the first value by one period, so CF0 is added outside the function.

q.q: When the discount rate increases, the NPV of a project with normal cash flows:
q.explain: Higher rate → smaller NPV; it crosses zero at the IRR.

q.q: Why does the course call subliminal perception a myth?
options: A stimulus below the absolute threshold never reaches the sensory receptors, so it cannot be processed
Because it only works on television
q.explain: No evidence of effect on behaviour (Vicary, 1957).

q.q: You shop for a car and suddenly notice car ads everywhere. This is:
q.explain: Vigilance: we notice stimuli related to current needs.

q.q: In semiotics, the Nike Swoosh is the:
q.explain: Object = the shoe/brand; sign = the Swoosh; interpretant = hip-hop culture, urban status symbol.

q.q: According to Krishna et al. (2010):
options: Ambient scent beats product scent for memory
Product scent is more effective than ambient scent for memory retention
Scent has no effect on memory
Scent only works in food stores
q.explain: Product scent improves memory retention more.

q.q: In Yalch & Spangenberg (1993), which condition gave the highest purchase rate?
q.explain: 76.0% in the men area with high tempo (vs 57.0% slow-women, 54.0% slow-men, 26.0% high-women).

q.q: A McDonald’s logo alone triggers hunger after being repeatedly paired with burgers. The logo is the:
q.explain: After pairing: CS → CR.

q.q: A loyalty scheme gives bigger prizes as you spend more. This applies:
q.explain: Rewards strengthen the behaviour: positive reinforcement.

q.q: A consumer buys a product after seeing a celebrity reward from it. Which learning type, and which first step?
q.explain: Observational learning (modeling): attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation.

q.q: Which transfer moves information from short-term to long-term memory?
q.explain: Attention moves sensory → short-term; elaboration moves short-term → long-term.

q.q: Which statement about retro brands is correct?
options: They are updated versions of products or identities from a prior period blending past aesthetics with present innovation
q.explain: Examples on the slide: Bonne Maman, Fiat 500.

q.q: Which is true of the absolute vs differential threshold?
options: Absolute = minimum detectable stimulus; differential = minimum detectable difference between two stimuli (j.n.d.)
q.explain: Thresholds vary from person to person and with context and attention.

q.q: Which of the following is listed as a support function in the course?
q.explain: Support: technological development, HRM, infrastructure.

q.q: In the ‘typical situation’, why does the sustainable product conflict with the company?
options: The management system (evaluation criteria, bonuses, spare parts) pushes in another direction
The product is too expensive to design
q.explain: Purchasing judged on price, engineers on time-to-market, sales on new units, no spare parts.

q.q: Which statement on the Apple value chain is in the slides?
options: Production is in the USA to reduce delays
Returns are allowed within 14 days if bought from an Apple store
It has only one distribution channel
q.explain: 14-day returns: very high costs but supports close ties with customers.

q.q: How many blocks does the BMC have, and what drives the creative process?
q.explain: Nine blocks; the process is value-driven.

q.q: According to Acosta et al. (2014), sustainable innovation is mainly seen as:
options: A compromise between economy and environment
An opportunity to optimise economic, social and environmental aspects simultaneously
q.explain: Not a compromise but an opportunity.

q.q: Which strategy is associated with a ‘risk of contestability: greenwashing or real commitment?’
q.explain: Strategy 2 (temporary project) shows that risk, plus integration/durability issues.

q.q: What are the two risk questions the value chain analysis asks about a function that creates little value but costs money?
options: Can we reduce costs/margins without risk? Can we externalize it without risk?
Can we advertise it? Can we patent it?
Can we raise prices? Can we hire more?
Can we copy competitors? Can we insure it?
q.explain: Slide 16.

sociology-social-transformations-managem.t: Economics — The Major Schools of Thought

q.q: Aristotle’s chrematistikē is:
options: Managing the household for a good life
Money-making for its own sake, limitless and judged unnatural
q.explain: Oikonomia has a natural limit; chrematistikē does not.

q.q: “Build it and demand will come” is associated with:
q.explain: Say’s Law; the slide calls it often dangerously wrong.

q.q: Which statement about Smith fits the course?
options: He was a moral philosopher who grounded markets in sympathy and trust
q.explain: Theory of Moral Sentiments.

q.q: For Marx, the surplus value captured by capital is:
q.explain: Value comes from labour; distribution is a relation of power.

q.q: Pareto efficiency means:
options: No one can be better off without someone worse off, and it says nothing about fairness
q.explain: Powerful but idealized.

q.q: Keynes’s “animal spirits” refer to:
q.explain: Radical uncertainty → investment swings on confidence.

q.q: Which school: value from marginal utility, self-regulating market at equilibrium, state corrects failures only?
q.explain: Row ‘Neoclassical’ of the synthesis table.

q.q: Ostrom’s contribution was to show that:
options: Communities can govern commons successfully under design principles
The state must own all resources
q.explain: She refuted the inevitability of Hardin’s tragedy.

q.q: A daycare fined late parents and lateness rose. This illustrates:
options: Motivation crowding-out: the fine turned a duty into a price
q.explain: Money can destroy the meaning that sustained the behaviour.

q.q: Axelrod’s tournaments found that in repeated games:
q.explain: Hence coopetition; most business is repeated.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the three reasons economists disagree?
q.explain: Meta-lesson: assumptions, values, performativity.

q.q: The 1970 Friedman doctrine is the root of:
q.explain: Now fiercely contested (Danone & Faber, 2021).

q.q: Which formula gives the project operating cash flow in the course?
q.explain: OCF = EBIT − Taxes + Depreciation.

q.q: Which item must NOT be included in the incremental cash flows of a project?
options: A change in net working capital
A side effect on other products
q.explain: Sunk costs are past and irreversible; the decision cannot affect them.

q.q: Why are interest and debt principal excluded from project cash flows?
options: The discount rate already accounts for financing costs
q.explain: The discount rate takes care of the financing costs.

q.q: Norma Desmond: sales 50,000, variable costs 30,000, fixed 5,000, depreciation 3,000, tax 34%. OCF is:
q.explain: EBIT 12,000 + depreciation 3,000 − taxes 4,080 = 10,920.

q.q: The machine (book value 12,000 after 3 years) is sold for 15,000 with a 34% tax rate. The tax on the sale is:
q.explain: (15,000 − 12,000) × 34% = 1,020, which reduces the cash received.

q.q: The $10,000 net working capital investment in the Norma Desmond example is:
q.explain: NWC is invested at t=0 (−10,000) and recaptured at the end of the project (+10,000).

q.q: In the indirect method, depreciation is:
q.explain: It is non-cash, so it is added back to net income.

q.q: Which statement on depreciation is in the course?
options: Land can be depreciated over 31.5 years
q.explain: The 1986 Tax Reform Act’s MACRS lets firms front-load depreciation; land cannot be depreciated.

q.q: “The customer always chooses the cheapest option” is, in Schein’s model, an example of:
q.explain: Implicit beliefs = fundamental assumptions.

q.q: A company presents ‘recyclable packaging’ but ignores impacts at other life-cycle stages. Which greenwashing mechanism?
q.explain: Slide 14: hidden impact transfer.

q.q: What distinguishes a ‘green organizational culture’ from a sustainability culture?
options: Green culture covers environmental, social and economic issues
Green culture focuses only on the environment
q.explain: Do not mix them up (slide 13).

q.q: In the IKEA example, what does the transformation require?
options: Transforming the entire value creation system
Stopping sales of new furniture immediately
q.explain: Sustainable innovation is not just greener products.

q.q: Which is NOT one of Goffee & Jones’ sources of inspiration?
q.explain: The four are: situational awareness, strong empathy, recognise strengths/weaknesses, dare to be different.

q.q: In Rehman & Zeb (2023), which hypotheses were rejected?
q.explain: AL → trust & safety (H2) and its mediation (H6) were rejected.

q.q: Which statement matches Yukl’s definition?
options: Leadership = influencing (shared understanding) and facilitating (conditions to act)
Leadership is only the vision of the top manager
q.explain: Two functions of leadership.

q.q: Assoratgoon & Kantabutra found that the least-studied cultural level in SOC research is:
q.explain: The assumption level (normative grounding) is the most lacking.

consumer-behavior-customer-experience-ma.t: The Self, Personality & the Body — Self-Empowerment through Brands

q.q: According to self-concept theory, a bigger gap between actual self and ideal self leads to:
q.explain: “The bigger the gap, the lower the self-esteem.”

q.q: In Goffman’s theatrical metaphor, a person carefully managing their image in public is on:
q.explain: Front stage: plays a role; back stage: vigilance relaxes.

q.q: Which comparison is described as the most common everyday benchmark?
q.explain: Lateral: peers similar in status or skill.

q.q: A bicycle-theft victim says the thief stole “a piece of my life”. This illustrates:
options: The extended self (losing possessions = losing self)
q.explain: Belk (1988): burglary and disaster victims grieve like mourning a loved one.

q.q: A taller avatar boosting real-world confidence is called the:
q.explain: Belk (2013), reembodiment.

q.q: Which Freudian component is the “conscience” internalizing society’s rules?
q.explain: Id = pleasure; ego = reality; superego = morality.

q.q: A consumer who “moves against others” (needs power, success, admiration) is, in Horney’s model:
q.explain: Aggressive types favour status/performance products (CAD scale, Cohen 1967).

q.q: How is personality measured in trait theory?
q.explain: Unlike Freud’s clinical interpretation; e.g. the Big Five (Goldberg, 1990).

q.q: Body positivity is:
options: Altering the body to match the ideal
Rejecting the ideal itself and promoting acceptance of one’s body as it is
Ignoring beauty ideals in advertising only
q.explain: Body modification is the other response (tattoos, dieting, surgery…).

q.q: According to the course, challenging gender stereotypes builds brand equity only when it:
q.explain: Reinforcing feels safe and familiar; both can work.

q.q: Rolex and Ferrari mainly target which self-image?
q.explain: They project the success, power and prestige you want others to perceive. (Patagonia = social; Nike/Apple = ideal; IKEA = actual.)

q.q: Which is NOT one of Aaker’s five dimensions of brand personality?
q.explain: Sincerity, excitement, competence, sophistication, ruggedness.

q.q: Dove’s strategy illustrates which of the three brand strategies?
q.explain: Dove validates the actual self instead of pushing an unattainable ideal.

q.q: A new line of recyclable sweaters is an example of:
q.explain: It is what the organization produces and brings to market.

q.q: Part of an outcome that would have happened even without the intervention is called:
q.explain: Deadweight requires a baseline benchmark.

q.q: A street-lighting scheme lowers crime in one area but crime rises next door. This illustrates:
q.explain: The problem was moved elsewhere.

q.q: Patients – health: 60 × €1,000, deadweight 20%, attribution 20%, displacement 0%. Year-1 net impact?
Total discounted benefits 158,417 € for an investment of 100,000 €. The SROI ratio is:
Why is the caregivers’ quality-of-life score not given an extra financial proxy?
options: To avoid double counting the same outcome
q.explain: It is a complementary indicator for the burnout outcome.

q.q: In Hutchinson et al. (2020), why were five scenarios used?
options: Because they evaluated a type of intervention with a wide range of costs
q.explain: Costs ranged from a spinner knob to complex electronic controls.

q.q: Which statement about SROI ratios is correct (Hutchinson et al.)?
options: They can be compared across any studies
They are context specific and not generalisable
q.explain: Pathak & Dattani (2014) cited in the article.

q.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Esprit de finesse: logic and calculation
Esprit de géométrie: logic and calculation
q.explain: Finesse is the intuitive, holistic judgment.

q.q: “The data will tell us what to do” is impossible mainly because of:
options: Hume: you cannot derive ought from is
q.explain: The ought is always your value choice.

q.q: “Order first, trust later” corresponds to:
q.explain: Strong authority (Leviathan).

q.q: “Treat employees and customers as ends, never merely as means” is:
q.explain: “Kant in the boardroom”.

q.q: Cost-benefit analysis is described in the course as applied:
q.explain: Ask who bears the cost of the greatest good.

q.q: In the trolley dilemma, the Kantian answer is that:
options: You may not use a person merely as a means, even to save five
q.explain: Duty constrains the calculus; the utilitarian pulls the lever.

q.q: For Arendt, violence is:
options: Merely instrumental and a sign that power has failed
q.explain: Power = acting in concert; authority = legitimacy without coercion.

q.q: Foucault’s panopticon applied to management means:
options: Open-plan offices and dashboards can make people police themselves
q.explain: Design them consciously.

q.q: Habermas’s ideal speech situation requires:
options: Open, undistorted dialogue among equals where the better argument prevails
q.explain: Legitimacy needs fair deliberation, not only optimality.

q.q: The ‘robust test’ for a just decision is that it:
options: Survives virtue, duty and consequences lenses; conflict reveals the real dilemma
q.explain: Slide 32.

q.q: Lyotard’s postmodern condition is:
q.explain: Plural, local, competing narratives.

q.q: Which question belongs to the philosophical compass?
q.explain: Compass: truth, values, ethics, legitimacy, power.
